content: 1. The decision-support logic embedded in the software system is customized and adapted based on validated decision-making frameworks to ensure its relevance and accuracy. 2. User testing is conducted among targeted populations to optimize the user experience and ensure the system meets the needs of its intended users. 3. Feedback from user testing is used to refine the intervention, ensuring that the system requirements and contextual factors, such as the use of mobile phones or tablets by health workers, are adequately addressed. 4. Computers are utilized to monitor the performance of the decision-support system, including the generation of reports and dashboards. 5. Initial training involves the development or adaptation of training curricula and standard operating procedures (SOPs) for using the decision-support system. 6. Health workers interacting with the decision-support system undergo initial training to ensure they can effectively use the software. 7. Supervisory staff are trained on SOPs and continuous monitoring, including tasks such as assessing software stability, algorithm functionality, and troubleshooting system failures. 8. Refresher training is provided periodically to health workers to reinforce their skills in using the decision-support system. 9. Supervisory staff also receive refresher training on continuous monitoring and the use of data generated by the system. 10. Periodic review meetings are held to discuss feedback on system performance and address any challenges encountered. 11. Technology maintenance includes software updates, license fees, and hardware maintenance, such as insurance and replacement of devices. 12. Ongoing adaptation and updates to the decision-support logic are implemented as new clinical practices or recommendations emerge. 13. Evidence suggests that digital tracking of clients’ health status and services via mobile devices can have both positive and negative effects. However, there is limited or no direct evidence on outcomes such as health worker or patient satisfaction, data quality, resource use, or unintended consequences. 14. Health workers often perceive digital health interventions as tools that enable them to perform more tasks, reach more people, and work more efficiently. These interventions are also seen as enhancing their social status. 15. Concerns among health workers include increased workload and, in some cases, personal expenses associated with using digital tools. Those who struggle with the technology may view it negatively and worry about job security. 16. Digital technologies are generally seen as advantageous compared to paper-based systems, offering quicker data recording, easier access to client information, and simpler correction of errors. However, some health workers prefer paper systems, citing trustworthiness and reduced risk of data loss. 17. When digital interventions require client registration, some health workers may view this as a menial task inappropriate for their professional level, leading to dissatisfaction and perceptions of increased workload. 18. Feasibility challenges for digital health interventions include issues with network connectivity, access to electricity, system integration, device usability, and health worker training. 19. Digital tracking via mobile devices may be particularly beneficial for clients with family or work responsibilities, those living far from healthcare facilities, and those with limited financial resources. However, access may be difficult for clients with poor network or electricity access, low literacy or digital skills, or stigmatized health conditions. 20. mLearning (mobile learning) interventions may increase healthcare professionals’ knowledge of health issue management, though evidence on other outcomes, such as provider performance or health behavior, is limited or uncertain. 21. Health workers and students appreciate mLearning tools for their ability to guide clinical practice, reduce reliance on memory, and address knowledge gaps. These tools are particularly valued in settings where senior advisors are unavailable. 22. Students may also value the ability to contact supervisors remotely via text or chat, though some clinicians prefer alternative methods, such as personal computers or paper, for teaching and assessments. 23. Digital tools are seen as enhancing professional identity, with students perceiving themselves and others as more competent when using these devices to retrieve information. 24. Cooperative learning opportunities facilitated by digital devices, such as online study groups and clinical discussion forums, are appreciated by students for their ability to resolve clinical questions and foster collaboration.
